newsitem.title: MEXICO: Two Mexican generals said linked to drug lord.
newsitem.headline: Two Mexican generals said linked to drug lord.

text.p: Two generals and the private secretary of former Mexican president Carlos Salinas de Gortari have been accused of links with Mexico's top drug kingpin Amado Carrillo Fuentes, the Mexican daily Reforma said on Thursday.

Juan Galvan Lara, a key witness who has already incriminated Mexico's former drug czar Gen. Jesus Gutierrez Rebollo as a cartel collaborator, made the claim in testimony to a military court in February, the daily added.
The Defence Ministry and Attorney-General's office both declined to comment on the report, the latest in a string of revelations about alleged drug links in the Mexican military.
Reforma printed a partial copy of what it said was a statement made to investigators by Galvan Lara, Gen. Gutierrez Rebollo's former driver.

"In the declarations made on Feb. 19...he noted that four generals, two now dead, and the private secretary of Carlos Salinos de Gortari, who was not named, had ties to members of the Juarez Cartel," Reforma said.

Salinas's secretary helped Eduardo Gonzalez Quirarte, a senior aide of drug lord Carrillo Fuentes, and his brothers find a house in a wealthy district of Mexico City, the daily quoted Galvan Lara as saying.

In his evidence linking the generals to Carrillo Fuentes' operations, Galvan Lara said Gonzalez Quirarte had contacts with personnel at an airbase in Mexico's Jalisco state, as did the four generals, Velarde Quinteo, Moucel Luna, Vincio Santoyo Feria and Gonzalo Curiel, the last two of whom are dead.

Gen. Gutierrez Rebollo, sacked in February as chief of Mexico's now defunct anti-narcotics agency for allegedly taking bribes from Carrillo Fuentes, was commander of the military region which included Jalisco until his appointment as Mexico's top drug fighter in December 1996. He is currently in jail while twin military and civilian hearings unfold.

His arrest provoked Mexico's the most serious drug corruption scandal, and has worried anti-drug officials in Washington who fear that secret drug intelligence they shared with the general may now be in cartel hands.
Gen. Feria died in still unexplained circumstances in May last year while Curiel was killed in September 1995 in a plane crash during a military air display.
